opus-5.5.text:
Well, the honest answer is that it was the path of least resistance. Turing completeness is one of those boxes people expect you to tick when you propose a new language. If you don't, the first question from a reviewer is "but can it compute everything?" So you want a clean, short argument, and Siegelmann and Sontag already did the heavy lifting back in the nineties. They showed that recurrent neural networks with rational weights can simulate a Turing machine. TensorLogic can express RNNs very directly, since an RNN is just a few tensor equations applied over time. So the proof becomes almost a one-liner: TensorLogic can represent an RNN, RNNs are Turing complete, done.

Now, why do I say it has no practical significance? Because that construction relies on things you'd never do in practice. You're encoding the entire tape of the Turing machine in the digits of a rational number, and you need unbounded precision to make it work. No real neural network runs that way. Floating point kills it immediately. So the result tells you about expressiveness in principle, not about what you'd actually build.

And frankly, I think Turing completeness is overrated as a criterion. Lots of things are Turing complete by accident: Magic: The Gathering, PowerPoint animations, you name it. The interesting question isn't whether a language can in principle compute everything. It's whether it lets you express the things you care about naturally, compactly, and efficiently. For TensorLogic, the real point is that it unifies neural and symbolic AI. Logical rules and tensor operations turn out to be the same thing, an Einstein summation. That's where the significance lies.

So I used Siegelmann because it was the most economical way to dispatch an objection. It's a formality. I could have done a more direct construction, simulating a Turing machine with tensor equations over a tape, and that's not hard either. But why reinvent the wheel when a well-known result gets you there in a paragraph? The paper's energy is better spent on the things that actually matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Siegelmann and Sontag’s result makes the proof “almost a one-liner” and was the most economical way to establish Turing completeness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, partly it's a matter of what's cheap. Siegelmann and Sontag showed back in the nineties that a recurrent network with rational weights and a saturating linear activation is Turing complete, and that construction maps almost directly onto what TensorLogic already has. Tensor Logic is Einstein summation plus a nonlinearity, and a recurrent net is exactly that: a matrix multiply, a nonlinearity, iterate. So once you have those pieces, the Turing completeness result comes for free. You just point at the construction and say, there, done. If I'd gone through a tensor encoding of lambda calculus or built a Turing machine out of logical rules, that would have been a longer proof and it wouldn't have told you anything more.

But the more important reason is that I wanted to make a point about what Turing completeness does and doesn't buy you. People love to say "my framework is Turing complete" as if that settled something. It doesn't. Lots of things are Turing complete, including things that are completely useless for doing AI. The Siegelmann construct is actually a perfect illustration of that, because it's a neural network that computes anything in principle and in practice nobody has ever used it for anything. It relies on encoding the whole tape into the arbitrary-precision digits of one number, which is exactly what you can't do in floating point. So by using it, I'm saying: yes, this box is checked, and here is why checking the box is not what matters.

What matters is whether the language lets you express the things you actually need to express, compactly and in a way that compiles down to efficient tensor operations. That's where the real content of TensorLogic is. Logic programs, probabilistic graphical models, kernel machines, transformers, all of those are a few lines of tensor equations, and they run on the GPU with no special machinery. The Turing completeness result is there so no one can say the language is fundamentally limited. But if I thought that was the interesting part, I would have spent more than a paragraph on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the Siegelmann construction maps almost directly onto TensorLogic, so the completeness result “comes for free,” while alternatives would require a longer proof.

astra-6.text:
Because those are two different questions. One is whether TensorLogic can, in principle, express arbitrary computation. The other is whether that particular construction is a useful way to perform computation in practice. A construction can settle the first question without being useful for the second.

The appeal of using the Siegelmann construction is that it gives us an existing route to a universality result: show that TensorLogic can express that construction, and Turing completeness follows. You don’t need to invent a new proof from scratch.

But Turing completeness is a very low bar for a programming language. It doesn’t tell you whether programs are efficient, whether they’re easy to write, or whether you can learn them from data. Those are the interesting practical questions. So the construction serves as a theoretical check on expressiveness; it isn’t a proposal for how people should actually build TensorLogic programs.

r001.rationale: The response says the Siegelmann construction offers an existing route to the result, so TensorLogic need only express it and no proof must be invented from scratch—communicating the brief proof rationale.

sol-6.1.text:
Because those are two different questions: whether a language is computationally universal, and whether the construction used to prove that is useful in practice. The Siegelmann construction gives you a direct route to the first: show that TensorLogic can express the recurrent network in that construction, and Turing completeness follows.

That doesn’t mean you should implement programs by encoding a Turing machine into a recurrent neural network. It’s an existence proof, not an implementation strategy. The practical question is whether TensorLogic makes useful algorithms easy to express, learn, and execute efficiently. Turing completeness by itself tells you very little about that.

r001.rationale: The response says the Siegelmann construction gives a direct route to proving Turing completeness, but it does not say the argument is very brief.
